title: Isaac Ruddell and the Guns at Ruddell’s Station
summary: In June 1780 British cannon broke the walls of Ruddell’s Station on the South Fork of Licking in Harrison County, and Capt. Isaac Ruddell surrendered.
bodyMarkdown:
In spring 1779 Capt. [Isaac Ruddell](/people/#isaac-ruddell) rebuilt a fort on the South Fork of Licking in today's Harrison County. The site was not new. John Hinkston had settled it in 1775 and abandoned it the next year. Ruddell's new post was called Ruddell's Station, or Fort Liberty.

Families came quickly, many of them Pennsylvania Germans. Martin's Station rose a few miles away. Together they made a small cluster of settlement north of the Bluegrass, close to the Licking route Native war parties used.

That route also served the British. In June 1780 [Capt. Henry Bird](/people/#henry-bird) came south from Detroit with Canadian volunteers, hundreds of Native allies, and something Kentucky had never faced, which was cannon. His force landed at the [Licking forks at Falmouth](/stories/falmouth-at-the-licking-forks/) and marched south.

Log walls could stop rifle balls but not artillery. When Bird's guns opened on Ruddell's Station, the shots cracked the stockade. Ruddell had no way to hold out, and he surrendered under a promise that the captives would be protected.

The promise did not hold. Warriors rushed in and took prisoners for themselves, and some settlers were killed. Martin's Station fell next, with little more resistance. The [American Battlefield Trust](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/revolutionary-war/battles/ruddells-station) counts roughly four hundred captives marched north toward Detroit and the Native towns.

Two of Ruddell's sons were adopted by the Shawnee. One, Stephen, grew up alongside Tecumseh and later lived as his companion, and in later life became a Baptist preacher who worked among the Shawnee.

Bird turned back rather than push on. News that [George Rogers Clark](/people/#george-rogers-clark) was gathering men helped hurry the retreat, and Clark struck the Shawnee towns that August. The British never again brought that scale of artillery into Kentucky. Two years later the fight moved to [Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) and [Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/).

## Kentucky today

State historical marker #107, "Ruddle's Station," stands on US 27 about four miles south of [Cynthiana](/stories/cynthiana-cynthia-anna-on-the-licking/). It uses the older spelling and sums up the site's life: settled by Hinkston in 1775, rebuilt by Ruddle in 1779, destroyed by Bird in 1780. In Falmouth, markers #34 and #953 tell where Bird's force landed.
